basic_info.name: MediKiosk (rohit-h11/medikiosk-sih-26047)
basic_info.description: This is a competing SIH 2026 Problem Statement 26047 team repository: an AI patient case-taking and pre-consultation summary platform for the Ministry of Ayush / AIIA, built as a 6-day hackathon MVP by a team of 5 ML engineers plus 1 full-stack developer. It is cloud-first: a FastAPI backend with a React (Vite) kiosk/doctor frontend, Supabase Postgres with pgvector for retrieval, and almost all intelligence provided by hosted APIs - Groq LPUs running a Qwen-27B dialogue model, Google Gemini 3.6 Flash for OCR and final summary synthesis, Sarvam AI for ASR/TTS, and sentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-dim) for embeddings. The single most load-bearing fact is that, despite README claims of 'FHIR-compliant clinical summaries' and bilingual structured output, the actually implemented summary artifact is a custom Pydantic JSON object called a ClinicalSummaryTicket; there is no NRCeS FHIR IG profile validation, no OPConsultRecord Composition/Bundle, and the README's advertised `/api/v1/summary` endpoint does not exist - the live implementation is a 5-endpoint `/api/v1/dialogue/*` and `/api/v1/ocr/*` suite. Its strongest differentiators are AYUSH depth (2,910 NAMASTE morbidity codes embedded in pgvector, a CCRAS Prakriti scale implementation, ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow grounding) and a two-phase design (fast streaming dialogue, then a deep multi-system summary). Its critical weakness against MediKiosk's hard constraints is that it is entirely dependent on cloud services, with no offline capability, no India data-residency guarantee stated, and no NRCeS/ABDM summary emission - and it produces differential diagnoses, drug-herb safety advice and treatment/diet plans, which sits close to the 'elicit, never diagnose' line MediKiosk must not cross.
basic_info.organization: Independent student/hackathon team, not a company: GitHub user rohit-h11 with contributors WAonTC2, vedantg1908-cmyk, hardik23jain-glitch and gmkulk-netizen. No institution, company, NGO or government affiliation is stated. The repository carries no organization, no website link and no license. It is not affiliated with the Ministry of Ayush or AIIA; those are the problem-statement sponsors only.
basic_info.country: India (SIH 2026, Problem Statement 26047, Ministry of Ayush / All India Institute of Ayurveda). Content, languages and standards are India-specific.
basic_info.status: Research / active hackathon prototype. Last commit 2026-09-06 (10 days before this verification), 43 commits, 16 open issues, 0 stars, 0 forks, issue creation restricted. Actively evolving through early September 2026 (new endpoints, Gemini/Groq two-phase pipeline, NAMASTE vector ingestion), but not a deployed product and not clinically validated. [uncertain]

technical_features.what_it_does: The platform provides a patient-facing OPD kiosk that conducts adaptive multilingual (voice plus touch) history-taking, OCR-digitizes prior prescriptions/lab reports, and generates a physician-ready structured summary. The implemented pipeline is a two-phase design: Phase 1 streams short conversational SOCRATES questions token-by-token from Groq-hosted Qwen-27B (with touch-screen option chips) until the SOCRATES slots are filled or a turn cap is reached, while a deterministic regex/rule red-flag interceptor screens each utterance for emergencies; Phase 2 (triggered on completion) has Google Gemini 3.6 Flash synthesize the full dialogue plus OCR context into a 'ClinicalSummaryTicket' - a five-layer JSON containing a SOCRATES HPI narrative, an Ayurvedic assessment (NAMASTE code, dosha imbalance, srotas, Agni, CCRAS Prakriti tendency, chikitsa principles), an allopathic differential with ICD-10 codes, a drug-herb safety cross-screen, and Pathya/Apathya dietary guidance. The ticket is displayed to the doctor and optionally printed as a QR consultation pass. It also exposes a doctor Q&A path over pgvector-based cross-visit patient history. Crucially, 'summarization' here is an LLM writing a diagnostic-adjacent clinical assessment, not a deterministic renderer of elicited slots into a standards-profiled document: the output is a bespoke JSON schema, not a FHIR Composition/Bundle, and no NRCeS/ABDM profile is emitted.
technical_features.architecture: Cloud-first three-subsystem architecture. Backend: FastAPI (Python 3.10+) with Pydantic schemas, JWT auth/RBAC, CORS/security middleware, deployed via uvicorn. Frontend: React + Vite kiosk UI and doctor dashboard. Data: Supabase Postgres with the pgvector extension; tables include clinical_reference_vectors (static guidelines) and patient_structured_vectors (per-patient document chunks), each with 384-dim embeddings from sentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and HNSW cosine indexes; SQL RPCs match_clinical_guidelines and match_patient_history (patient-scoped, with temporal recency decay); Supabase Auth for staff and Supabase Storage for WebP images. Models via hosted APIs: Groq LPU Qwen-27B for streaming dialogue; Google Gemini 3.6 Flash for Vision OCR and structured summary function-calling; Sarvam AI (Saaras ASR, Bulbul TTS) plus Bhashini/Indic TTS; AI4Bharat IndicConformer/IndicWhisper for ASR and IndicTrans2 for Hindi/English translation in the documented 'translate-then-reason' design. Static knowledge ingestion uses PyMuPDF heuristics plus an LLM extractor to turn NAMASTE morbidity Excel data, the CCRAS Prakriti tool, WHO Traditional Medicine benchmarks and ICMR Standard Treatment Workflows into atomic 120-240 word chunks. There is no on-prem/edge inference path: all LLM, OCR, TTS and database work is remote.
technical_features.inputs: Patient speech (browser push-to-talk WebAudio, captured client-side with Web DSP noise/rumble removal) and touch-screen option selections; patient demographics, age, gender, chief complaint, symptoms, past medical history, current medications, allergies and vitals supplied to /dialogue/start; photographs of prior documents (prescription/lab report/discharge summary) compressed client-side to ~2048px WebP; prior document context retrieved from pgvector; ABHA sandbox credentials (OTP) for patient identity; static knowledge-base chunks (NAMASTE, CCRAS, ICMR STW, WHO TM benchmarks).
technical_features.outputs: A custom JSON 'ClinicalSummaryTicket' (Pydantic model) containing triage urgency, vitals, chief complaint, SOCRATES HPI narrative, Ayurvedic assessment with NAMASTE code, allopathic differential with ICD-10 codes, drug-herb safety screening, Pathya/Apathya dietary guidelines, suggested investigations and doctor consultation notes; per-turn dialogue JSON with next question, touch options and SOCRATES slot state; SSE token streams for TTS; OCR extraction JSON with diagnoses/medications/lab flags and 384-dim vector chunks; a kiosk summary card plus thermal-printed QR consultation pass; and a doctor dashboard ticket via GET /api/v1/doctor/ticket/{id}. The README and spec additionally claim a 'FHIR R4 JSON' / 'FHIR-shaped JSON' export, but no implemented FHIR Composition/Bundle or NRCeS profile artifact was found in the code or docs read. [uncertain]
technical_features.standards_compliance: [uncertain] Claims are substantially ahead of demonstrated validation. The README asserts design 'in accordance with ABDM standards and DPDP Act 2023' and AYUSH mapping to 'NAMASTE/ICD-11'; the project spec targets NAMASTE (National AYUSH Morbidity and Standardized Terminologies) mapped to WHO ICD-11 Chapter 26 Module 2 (TM2) and mentions the open-source AyushSyncAPI FHIR R4 NAMASTE<->ICD-11 bridge; the ROADMAP lists 'Verify NAMASTE to WHO ICD-11 (TM2) code mapping accuracy' as a Day 5 task. However, the newer implementation docs consistently use ICD-10 (not ICD-11) codes, and the actual implemented summary is a custom ClinicalSummaryTicket - there is no evidence of FHIR R4 profile validation against the NRCeS FHIR Implementation Guide (v6.5.0) or the OPConsultRecord Composition, and no FHIR Bundle.type=document artifact. ABDM is targeted via an ABHA sandbox OTP flow with a mock fallback, not a validated HIP/HIU integration. DPDP Act 2023 compliance is claimed (AES-256 document encryption at rest, SHA-256 integrity hashing, consent-record hashing, crypto-erasure by key deletion) but is self-declared, not audited. Terminology depth (2,910 NAMASTE codes) is real in the vector store, but the code-system labelling is internally inconsistent (ICD-11 in README/spec vs ICD-10 in pipeline docs). Net: NAMASTE/ICD-11/ABDM conformance is claimed and partially built (ABHA sandbox, NAMASTE vectors) but NRCeS profile conformance is not validated, and the ICD version used is ambiguous.
technical_features.offline_capability: None. The architecture is explicitly cloud-first and requires connectivity for essentially every function: dialogue generation (Groq LPUs), summary synthesis and Vision OCR (Google Gemini Flash), speech recognition and voice synthesis (Sarvam AI / Bhashini), embeddings and retrieval (Supabase pgvector), storage (Supabase Storage) and staff auth (Supabase Auth). There is no local model, no on-device inference, no local encrypted store, no store-and-forward queue and no offline sync or merge. The only local processing is client-side WebAudio noise reduction and image compression to WebP. This is a direct, structural conflict with MediKiosk's offline-first hard constraint and with the ~4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk target.
technical_features.languages_supported: Indian-language-first: Hindi (Devanagari), Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Bengali and English are offered in the kiosk language dropdown, with a 'translate-then-reason' design (IndicConformer/IndicWhisper ASR, IndicTrans2 bidirectional translation, English reasoning core, Sarvam Bulbul/Bhashini TTS). Live examples show Hindi speech synthesis and Devanagari text. Code-mixed Hinglish handling is not explicitly discussed. Physician summary is described as bilingual (local-language patient confirmation plus English/Hindi physician summary), though the implemented ClinicalSummaryTicket examples are English. Because all ASR/TTS/translation is hosted, language coverage is limited by API availability and connectivity.
technical_features.deployment_model: Cloud/SaaS with a thin client: FastAPI and Supabase run in the cloud (Supabase Postgres/pgvector/Auth/Storage); the kiosk and doctor dashboard are React (Vite) web apps served to browser-based kiosk touchscreens (localhost:5173 in dev). Setup scripts target Windows/PowerShell, macOS/Linux and Git Bash. No on-device model, no kiosk hardware specification, no CPU/GPU/RAM requirements and no offline deployment mode are published. Inference cost and behaviour depend on third-party API quotas (the docs note Groq free-tier rate limits).

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: [uncertain] All figures are self-claimed hackathon benchmarks, several of which are internally inconsistent and none peer-reviewed. Claims include: 100% emergency red-flag recall (40/40 emergencies, 0 false positives) in one doc but 98.7% (74/75 tests) in another, versus a claimed 64.2% plain-LLM baseline; 0.0% measured clinical hallucination error on a 19-atomic-claim audit (versus a 38.4% Med-HALT 2023 baseline) in one doc but 'less than 1.8%' hallucination in another; 100.0% deterministic CCRAS-SF-12 Prakriti classification match over 10,000 Monte Carlo profiles (9.07 microseconds each, p50 7.8us / p95 16.5us); 2,910 NAMASTE morbidity codes in the vector store versus 25-40 generic terms, framed as +11,540% coverage; SOCRATES clinical relevance 94.6/100 versus a 52.0/100 plain-LLM baseline; ~75% OPD time saved. These numbers are produced by the team's own scripts, are not independently reproducible from the repository data, and mix measured code benchmarks with literature-baseline comparisons.
performance_metrics.latency: Self-reported cloud latency budget: Groq Qwen-27B time-to-first-token ~280-300 ms, total voice-to-voice turn ~415 ms (dual vector search 8.4 ms + red-flag scan 1.2 ms + TTFT ~280 ms + SSE 15 ms + Sarvam TTS ~110 ms); static MCQ turns ~350 ms to 2.17 s; sentence-streaming TTFA under 700 ms; final Gemini 3.6 Flash summary generation 1.0-1.8 s (one doc cites 1,320 ms); pgvector HNSW query under 15 ms (measured ~8.42 ms); SHA-256 dedup hash 66.32 microseconds; WebP compression ~214.59 ms mean. These reflect cloud inference and network conditions, not a CPU-only kiosk, and are team-measured rather than externally benchmarked.
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: [uncertain] No kiosk or server hardware footprint is published. Because all AI and storage are hosted APIs/Supabase, the on-device requirement is only a browser (plus client-side WebAudio/image compression); there is no CPU/iGPU/RAM/model-size/storage figure for running the pipeline locally. Groq's free tier is noted to cap output tokens (e.g. 1,000 OTPM), implying quota dependence. The system cannot run on the MediKiosk ~4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk target as designed because it has no local inference path.
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: Adoption is near zero: 0 stars, 0 forks, 0 watchers, 43 commits, 16 open issues (none closed), issue creation restricted, 5 ML + 1 dev team, and a 6-day sprint. Internal build scale: 5 primary endpoints, 2,910 NAMASTE codes embedded, 2,978 vector cards (68 guideline sub-cards at ~144.7 mean words), a 10,000-profile Prakriti Monte Carlo run, and a 500-1,000 case triage benchmark. No real patients, clinics, records, sessions or installs are reported.
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: Self-run hackathon evaluation harnesses rather than peer-reviewed study: comprehensive_stress_benchmark.py (10,000 Monte Carlo Prakriti profiles, 60-case or 500-1,000-case triage confusion matrix, 25-sample image compression), benchmark_metrics.py (live ASGI endpoint latency, Supabase RPC timing, Sarvam TTS), run_large_scale_benchmark.py (async clinical vignette benchmark with an LLM cascade Groq -> Gemini -> OpenAI -> heuristic), a 14-test pytest suite across allopathy/Ayurveda protocols, and simulate_patient_flow.py. Dataset provenance is claimed from MedQA/USMLE vignettes, MIMIC-IV-ED, ICMR STW and CCRAS/AYUSH registries, but the datasets and results are not bundled for independent reproduction, the benchmarks appear partly LLM-synthetic, and no clinician adjudication or statistical significance testing is reported. The included clinical_benchmark_500_dataset.json is referenced by internal file paths, not published in the repo. Everything is vendor/team-claimed.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: This is the single most directly comparable SIH26047 competitor and therefore the most important reference for Module C's positioning and threat assessment. It validates several core assumptions: that an adaptive voice+touch SOCRATES intake is buildable in a hackathon window; that AYUSH depth (CCRAS Prakriti, NAMASTE coding, Pathya/Apathya) is the expected winning differentiator for the Ayush/AIIA problem; that retrieval-grounded summarization (not raw LLM generation) is the accepted hallucination-control story; and that a two-phase split - fast streaming dialogue for latency, then a slower, deep, multi-system synthesis pass - is a reasonable architecture. For Module C specifically it supplies a concrete picture of the competing summary artifact (a 5-layer ClinicalSummaryTicket with SOCRATES-HPI, NAMASTE+ICD differential, drug-herb safety, diet guidance, investigations) and of the doctor-delivery surface (pre-populated OPD ticket, QR consultation pass, doctor Q&A). It also exposes the gap MediKiosk must exploit: this competitor's summary is cloud-generated custom JSON with no NRCeS/ABDM profile, and it requires constant connectivity. It threatens MediKiosk only if judges weight AYUSH coding depth and demo polish above offline operation, data residency and standards-conformant emission - which are MediKiosk's hard constraints.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt (as ideas, re-implemented offline): (1) the clinical grounding strategy - retrieval over curated national sources (NAMASTE morbidity, CCRAS Prakriti, ICMR Standard Treatment Workflows, WHO Traditional Medicine benchmarks) is a sound way to expose an AYUSH-native summary without hallucination, and a small bundled/offline subset of these could seed Module C's terminology; (2) the two-phase latency design (fast streaming elicitation, then a deep synthesis pass) mapped to an offline equivalent; (3) the explicit SOCRATES slot-state machine with covered/missing slots as a deterministic scaffold the summary renderer consumes - this is exactly the MEDCOD/Note2Chat pattern and fits Module C's deterministic renderer; (4) the doctor-editable, pre-populated ticket plus QR/print handoff, which matches MediKiosk's physician-attestation workflow; (5) the two-RAG separation (national guidelines vs patient-specific history) and strict patient-scoped retrieval as a privacy pattern; (6) NAMASTE<->ICD-11 TM2 mapping intent. Reject: (1) cloud-only inference (Groq/Gemini/Sarvam/Supabase) - impossible on the 4GB CPU/iGPU offline kiosk; (2) the 'FHIR-shaped' custom JSON as the output contract - Module C must emit a validated NRCeS OPConsultRecord Composition/Bundle, not a bespoke ticket; (3) producing differential diagnoses, ICD codes, drug-herb interaction warnings and treatment/diet plans as if from an AI - this violates MediKiosk's elicit-never-diagnose and physician-attestation principles, and the competitor's own example prescribes formulations and Rxs, which Module C must not do; (4) unverifiable headline metrics and inconsistent numbers as evidence; (5) the unlicensed codebase (no LICENSE) for any reuse; (6) ICD-10 vs ICD-11 ambiguity.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: No license file exists, so the code is all-rights-reserved by default and unsafe to copy. The README is materially stale and overclaims: it advertises an /api/v1/summary endpoint that does not exist (the real endpoints are /api/v1/dialogue/* and /api/v1/ocr/*), and 'FHIR-compliant'/'FHIR R4 JSON' output that is in practice a custom ClinicalSummaryTicket. There is no NRCeS FHIR IG v6.5.0 validation and no OPConsultRecord artifact - the v6.5.0 profile-validation claim from the earlier research note did not harden; if anything the FHIR story regressed as the build focused on a custom ticket. Terminology claims are inconsistent (README/spec say NAMASTE/ICD-11 TM2; implementation docs use ICD-10) and access to the full official NAMASTE dataset was flagged as historically unreliable, so the '2,910 codes' figure needs independent verification. Performance metrics are self-claimed, internally contradictory (100% vs 98.7% recall; 0% vs <1.8% hallucination), partly derived from literature-baseline comparisons rather than measurement, and not independently reproducible. The system cannot operate offline at all, and there is no stated India data-residency guarantee for Supabase/Groq/Gemini/Sarvam processing. Clinically it drifts toward diagnosis and prescribing. It also carries the normal hackathon risks: 16 open issues, no closed issues, no tests published as results, and documentation that has outrun the implementation.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: MediKiosk and this competitor target the same problem but with opposite architectural commitments. MediKiosk: offline-first on a ~4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk with no discrete GPU, India data residency, NRCeS FHIR IG OPConsultRecord emission (Bundle.type=document) with a mandatory attester slot, per-field provenance, deterministic elicit-never-diagnose summarization, and explicit physician attestation. This competitor: cloud-only hosted APIs, no offline path, no stated residency, a custom ClinicalSummaryTicket instead of a validated FHIR profile, LLM-authored differential diagnoses and treatment/diet plans, and no license. The competitor does erode MediKiosk's differentiation on AYUSH depth - it has invested heavily in NAMASTE (2,910 codes), a CCRAS Prakriti scorer, ICMR STW grounding and a genuinely distinct Ayurvedic dialogue branch, which is likely the dimension judges will reward and which MediKiosk must match with a credible, offline, NRCeS-aligned equivalent. But it leaves MediKiosk's core claims intact and even sharpened: this competitor demonstrates that the offline + NRCeS + residency + attestation combination remains unoccupied, while showing exactly how much AYUSH terminology work is needed to be competitive. The strategic read is that MediKiosk should not compete on cloud polish or on diagnostic content, but should make its offline operation and validated NRCeS OPConsultRecord emission unmissable, and should close the AYUSH terminology gap with an offline NAMASTE/CCRAS subset.

business_info.license: No license file exists in the repository. The root directory listing contains no LICENSE, COPYING or NOTICE file, and the README only states 'Developed under Smart India Hackathon (SIH 2026) for Problem Statement 26047' with no license grant. Under default copyright, all rights are reserved; the code cannot be legally reused or redistributed without permission. This is a material risk if any part of this competitor's approach were to be copied.

competition_ecosystem.competitors: Direct competitors are other SIH 2026 PS26047 teams, including MediKiosk itself, as well as the India AI-medical-scribe/intake cohort (Eka Care/EkaScribe, Sunoh.ai, Augnito Omni, NirogStreet for AYUSH practitioners) and offline-ABDM tools such as CureNet that converge on the same offline+ABDM+FHIR space from the opposite (offline) direction. This repository does not compete with MediKiosk on offline operation or NRCeS emission but is a close competitor on AYUSH-native intake and summary depth. [uncertain]
competition_ecosystem.integrations: Supabase (Postgres + pgvector + Auth + Storage), Groq LPU inference, Google Gemini Vision/summary API, Sarvam AI (ASR/TTS) and Bhashini/Indic TTS, AI4Bharat IndicConformer/IndicWhisper and IndicTrans2, ABDM ABHA sandbox OTP flow (with a mock fallback), and pgvector RPCs for guideline and patient-history retrieval. Doctor/EMR delivery is described as a webhook or Supabase Realtime push rather than a named HIS integration; there is no validated ABDM HIP/HIU/PHR role, no Health Locker integration and no named hospital HIS vendor integration. [uncertain]
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: The context is the Ministry of Ayush / AIIA SIH 2026 problem, where the expected differentiators are AYUSH depth (CCRAS Prakriti, Dashavidha Pariksha, NAMASTE/ICD-11 TM2) plus a physician-ready summary. Two ecosystem facts matter for MediKiosk: (1) most competing teams, including this one, build cloud-first stacks with hosted LLM/ASR APIs, so offline operation on constrained hardware is a genuine, defensible differentiator rather than a commodity; (2) the AYUSH terminology and coding layer (NAMASTE, CCRAS, ICD-11 TM2) is becoming table stakes in this competition, and the Kiosk should ensure an offline-capable terminology subset and correct ICD version. The NRCeS FHIR IG for ABDM (v6.5.0, with OPConsultRecord) remains the sanctioned output contract and no PS26047 competitor observed has validated emission against it, leaving that lane open.

history.key_milestones: 2026-08-29: repository scaffold, project spec and 6-day ROADMAP, milestone issues opened (Aug 31 the first PRs merged). 2026-08-31 to 2026-09-01: transcript/dialogue work (Groq plus local model), OCR and prescription extraction pipeline, DOCS/schemas. 2026-09-02: RAG pipeline, SOCRATES dialogue framework implemented, ML3 dialogue manager with SOCRATES, CCRAS-PAS and a NAMASTE bridge (PR #28), vector-embedding pipeline merged. 2026-09-03: Sarvam TTS implemented, dialogue endpoint created, RAG-pipeline optimization. 2026-09-05: research docs, vector embedding pipeline enhancements, storing the full conversation at the end. 2026-09-06: merge PR #35, 'more docs', implementation changes (latest commit). Across the window the stack shifted from an early Sarvam-ASR/Llama-3.3 design to a two-phase Groq Qwen-27B + Gemini 3.6 Flash pipeline with a 5-endpoint API.
history.recent_changes_last_6_months: All activity is within the last 6 months and is concentrated in a short burst: 2026-08-29 to 2026-09-06, 43 commits, 16 open issues, 0 closed. Within that window the team moved to the current 5-endpoint suite (/ocr/process-document, /dialogue/stream-turn, /dialogue/turn, /dialogue/session/{id}, /doctor/ticket/{id}); switched the dialogue model to Groq-hosted Qwen-27B with Gemini 3.6 Flash for OCR and final summary; added per-document vector embedding into patient_structured_vectors; embedded 2,910 NAMASTE codes and the CCRAS Prakriti tool into pgvector; added a CCRAS-SF-12 Prakriti scorer and Dashavidha classification; and published extensive self-benchmark documentation. The currency check on the two specific items from the earlier research note is negative: no NRCeS FHIR IG v6.5.0 or OPConsultRecord profile validation was added (the FHIR export issue #15 is still open and the README's /api/v1/summary endpoint does not exist), and the CCRAS PAS / NAMASTE / ICD-11 claims were expanded in documentation and partially implemented as pgvector NAMASTE vectors, but did not harden into validated conformance - the ICD version is used inconsistently as ICD-10 in newer docs versus ICD-11 TM2 in the README/spec.

market_positioning.target_users: Patients (kiosk users, including non-literate and regional-language patients), allopathic doctors and AYUSH/Ayurvedic vaidyas reviewing pre-built summaries, hospital OPDs and Ayush wellness centres, and secondarily the SIH 2026 judges/administrators. Staff auth is via Supabase; patient identity via ABHA.
market_positioning.market_segment: Patient intake and pre-consultation clinical summarization for Indian OPDs, with an AYUSH/Ayurveda clinical-decision-support flavour - overlapping the intake, AYUSH software and ABDM/FHIR tooling segments rather than ambient scribing.
market_positioning.positioning_statement: The README pitches it as an 'AI Clinical History Software Platform' that 'solves this by serving as an AI-powered voice & touch intake kiosk used by patients before entering the consultation room', capturing 'adaptive clinical history in native Indian languages, digitizes physical records, extracts structured medical data, maps AYUSH diagnoses to NAMASTE/ICD-11 standards, and generates FHIR-compliant clinical summaries for immediate doctor review.' It emphasizes AYUSH-native dual dialogue (CCRAS Prakriti Assessment Scale plus SOCRATES), document digitization, a 30-second clinical summarizer, a doctor RAG assistant, rule-based red-flag triage and 'ABDM & DPDP Act 2023 Compliant' security. Several of these claims (FHIR-compliant summaries, the /api/v1/summary endpoint, NRCeS-conformant output) are aspirational rather than implemented.
